title: Lipoprotein(a) in Cardiovascular Disease: Integrating Epidemiology, Clinical Guidelines, Molar Measurement, and Emerging Therapies.
authors: Peter E Thomas; Signe Vedel-Krogh; Florian Kronenberg; Børge G Nordestgaard
abstract:
Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD = myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease) and aortic valve stenosis. Plasma concentrations of Lp(a) are >90% genetically determined. Multiple drugs in development reduce lipoprotein(a) by 80% to 98%. While the recently announced topline results, the phase 3 Lp(a)HORIZON trial of pelacarsen did not meet its primary cardiovascular endpoint despite lowering Lp(a), and 3 other cardiovascular outcomes trials remain ongoing. Lipoprotein(a) testing is currently increasing rapidly in many countries.
Most guidelines on dyslipidemia and prevention of cardiovascular disease worldwide now advise that Lp(a) should be measured once in all adults, ideally jointly with the first lipid profile ordered. If previous lipid profiles were taken, then Lp(a) should be included in the next lipid profile. Lipoprotein(a) should ideally be measured in nmol/L, and repeat measurements are relevant if drugs are given to lower Lp(a) concentrations, initially at suspected acute coronary syndrome or stroke and again after 1 month, and sometimes in women after menopause. Measuring Lp(a) levels alongside a standard lipid profile provides a more comprehensive initial assessment of a patient's overall cardiovascular risk. Clinical chemistry laboratories that measure lipid profiles should therefore also offer Lp(a) testing. This is easily done as Lp(a) assays can be run on most major clinical chemistry platforms. High Lp(a) is >105 nmol/L (>50 mg/dL).
As use of Lp(a) testing is increasing rapidly worldwide, more clinical chemistry laboratories will likely offer this test locally. Measuring Lp(a) levels alongside a standard lipid profile provides a more comprehensive initial lipid assessment of a patient's cardiovascular risk.

title: Pulse wave analysis detected by a computerized method using the cardio-ankle vascular index in aortic stenosis.
authors: Noriyasu Suzuki; Yusuke Suzuki; Yukiyo Ogata; Tomoyuki Kabutoya; Tatsuya Yoneyama; Yumi Nakagawa; Kyohei Fukatani; Satoshi Hoshide; Kazuomi Kario
journal: Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension
abstract: Although pulsus parvus et tardus is a classical physical finding in aortic stenosis (AS), objective quantitative assessment of pulse waveform morphology has been limited. We developed a novel computerized pulse waveform parameter, initial upstroke time (iUT), derived from cardio-ankle vascular index (CAVI) pulse waveforms to quantify the delay in the initial systolic upstroke. We analyzed 158 patients with mild or greater AS who underwent CAVI measurement and echocardiography. Associations of conventional upstroke time (UT) and iUT with echocardiographic measures of AS severity, including aortic valve area (AVA), peak aortic jet velocity (Vmax), and mean pressure gradient (MPG), were evaluated using multivariable regression analyses. Diagnostic performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic analysis. Both UT and iUT were significantly correlated with AVA and Vmax; however, iUT showed stronger correlations. In multivariable analyses including both parameters, iUT remained independently associated with AVA (standardized β = -0.488, P < 0.001) and Vmax (standardized β = 0.573, P < 0.001), whereas UT was not associated with Vmax and showed only a borderline association with AVA. Compared with UT, iUT also demonstrated superior diagnostic performance for identifying severe AS defined by Vmax ≥4.0 m/s (area under the curve [AUC], 0.843 vs. 0.678; P = 0.005) and MPG ≥ 40 mmHg (AUC, 0.795 vs. 0.637; P = 0.003), but not for AVA ≤ 1.0 cm². A novel computerized pulse waveform parameter reflecting the initial systolic upstroke was more strongly associated with echocardiographic measures of AS severity than conventional UT. Automated analysis of CAVI pulse waveforms may provide an objective adjunct for assessing AS without additional testing.

title: Prognostic Value of Tissue Doppler Late Diastolic Velocity (TDI-a') in Patients with Severe Aortic Stenosis Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation.
authors: Antonella Cecchetto; Roberta Bogoni; Francesco Zupa; Giuseppe Tarantini; Martina Perazzolo Marra; Domenico Corrado; Donato Mele; Stefano Nistri
abstract: Risk stratification after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in severe aortic stenosis (AS) remains suboptimal. Beyond valvular hemodynamics, a number of standard echocardiographic parameters of function are associated to outcome. Mitral annular late diastolic velocity (TDI-a') is proven to have prognostic value in multiple clinical settings, but its role after TAVI is unresolved. In a single-center retrospective observational study we included adult patients with isolated severe AS (aortic valve area < 1.0 cm²) undergoing TAVI, between December 2013 and August 2025. Pre-procedural transthoracic echocardiography was reviewed offline by blinded investigators to measure TDI-a' velocities. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. Logistic regression, Cox proportional hazards models, and ROC analysis were performed. A total of 805 patients (median age 81 years; 44.8% male) were included. During a median follow-up of 36.5 months, 196 deaths (24.3%) occurred. On univariable analysis, left ventricular ejection fraction, E/e' ratio, left atrioventricular coupling index (LACI), and TDI-a' were associated with mortality. In multivariable analysis, average TDI-a' remained the only independent echocardiographic predictor of mortality in both logistic regression (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.821-0.944; p < 0.001) and Cox analysis (HR 0.934, 95% CI 0.881-0.991; p = 0.023). ROC analysis showed modest discrimination (AUC 0.585), with an optimal cut-off ≤ 8.4 cm/s (sensitivity 65%, specificity 49%). Reduced TDI-a' is independently associated with mortality after TAVI, beyond conventional echocardiographic predictors. Despite modest discrimination, it is a simple prognostic marker that may improve pre-procedural risk stratification and warrants further prospective validation.
