title: Molecular signatures associated with reduced renal function in aortic regurgitation and aortic stenosis.
authors: Ernesto Martín-Núñez; Mattie Garaikoetxea; Alba Sádaba; Carolina Tiraplegui; Amaya Fernández de Celis; Blanca Otegui; Susana San Ildefonso-García; Miriam Goñi-Olóriz; Virginia Álvarez; Adela Navarro; Rafael Sádaba; Natalia López-Andrés
abstract:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) accelerates aortic valve (AV) disease, yet the molecular pathways linking declining renal function to aortic regurgitation (AR) and aortic stenosis (AS) remain poorly defined. We aimed to characterize AV phenotype-specific molecular signatures associated with reduced renal function.
We performed an observational cross-sectional study using targeted proteomic profiling (Olink) in human AV from patients with AR or AS, stratified by renal function (eGFR≥60 vs < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2). Pathway enrichment analyses were performed using exploratory candidate proteins. Candidate molecular signatures were subsequently examined in independent cohorts (AR: n = 215; AS: n = 325) across renal function categories using histology, immunohistochemistry, ELISA, and qPCR.
Reduced renal function was associated with distinct molecular patterns in AR and AS. In AR, exploratory proteomic profiling suggested enrichment of neutrophil degranulation, chemotaxis/adhesion and thrombo-inflammatory signaling pathways. Tissue characterization showed progressive extracellular matrix remodeling, collagen maturation, increased neutrophil markers (NGAL, MPO) and upregulation of pro-inflammatory (IL6, IL-8, IL-32, IL-33, CCL-2, TNF-α, RANTES), pro-adhesive (ICAM-1) and pro-thrombotic mediators (PAI-1) across renal function categories. In AS, exploratory proteomics suggested matrix disassembly and osteogenic signatures, while tissue characterization showed greater valvular calcification (BMP-2, -4, -9), collagen degradation (COL1, MMP-1, -3, TIMP-1) and inflammatory infiltration with declining renal function. Shared candidate proteins showed opposite regulation in AR and AS.
Reduced renal function is associated with distinct, phenotype-specific patterns of AV remodeling-predominantly thrombo-inflammatory in AR and osteogenic-matrix-disruptive in AS- indicating heterogeneous molecular responses across the two major forms of aortic valve disease.

title: Torsades de Pointes in Severe Aortic Stenosis: A Case Report of Nightmare Double-trouble.
authors: Pramod Kumar; Nikhat Parween; Sudipta Mondal; Nadeem Afroz Muslim
journal: The Journal of innovations in cardiac rhythm management
abstract:
Torsades de pointes (TdP) is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia arising in the setting of repolarization prolongation and is often facilitated by bradycardia-dependent mechanisms. Its management becomes particularly challenging in fixed-output physiology, where rate modulation may conflict with hemodynamic stability. Severe aortic stenosis (AS), especially when accompanied by left ventricular dysfunction, represents such a substrate, requiring a careful balance between electrical stabilization and preservation of forward flow. A 70-year-old woman with symptomatic severe AS and moderate left ventricular dysfunction underwent cardiac computed tomography for preoperative assessment. Immediately following contrast administration, she developed sinus bradycardia, marked QT prolongation (corrected QT, 560 ms), ventricular ectopy characterized by long-short sequences, and recurrent TdP with hemodynamic compromise. Intravenous magnesium and a single bolus dose of amiodarone were administered empirically; however, arrhythmia recurred and QT prolongation persisted. Electrolytes were within normal limits aside from low-normal potassium, which was subsequently corrected. In the setting of bradycardia-dependent TdP and a relative contraindication to aggressive β-blockade in a fixed-output state, semipermanent atrial pacing at 90 bpm was instituted. Rate acceleration suppressed ventricular ectopy and prevented further TdP episodes. Coronary angiography demonstrated no obstructive disease. The patient subsequently underwent urgent surgical aortic valve replacement but developed refractory ventricular fibrillation intraoperatively and could not be resuscitated. This case highlights repolarization vulnerability in structural heart disease, wherein bradycardia-dependent QT prolongation, pharmacologic influences, and procedural stress may converge to precipitate malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Recognition of rate-dependent mechanisms and judicious anti-arrhythmic selection are essential when managing electrical instability in structurally compromised hearts.
Torsades de pointes in patients with severe structural heart disease presents a unique therapeutic challenge when fixed-output physiology limits conventional rate and antiarrhythmic strategies. This case highlights an important and potentially underrecognized interaction between severe aortic stenosis, acquired QT prolongation, bradycardia, and procedural stress. The immediate onset after contrast administration suggests a trigger-substrate interaction rather than contrast exposure as an isolated cause. Importantly, recurrent bradycardia-dependent torsades was successfully suppressed by controlled atrial pacing at 90 beats/min, despite the hemodynamic constraints of severe aortic stenosis. The case also underscores the need to distinguish pause-dependent torsades from other forms of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, particularly because drugs such as amiodarone may worsen repolarization. Recognition of the underlying electrophysiologic mechanism and judicious use of pacing may be critical for stabilizing patients with malignant ventricular arrhythmias in structurally compromised hearts.

title: Precision medicine meets vascular disease: innovations in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis management.
authors: Ahnaf J Ahmed; Austin J Marrah; Trenton G Mayberry; Braydon C Cowan; Mark R Wakefield; Yujiang Fang
abstract: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS) is a significant cause of secondary hypertension and kidney injury with important cardiovascular consequences. This review briefly discusses the pathophysiology of ARAS, evaluates in-depth the diagnostic performance of duplex ultrasound, computed tomography angiography, and magnetic resonance angiography, and synthesizes results from major randomized trials and observational studies to explore current treatment options. The objective is to define the current diagnostic and therapeutic landscape of ARAS in a manner that supports evidence-based clinical decision making, and identify which treatment modality may be appropriate based on clinical presentation. The preference for optimized medical therapy as the initial standard of care is largely based on multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which found no overall benefit from invasive endovascular treatments in conjunction with medical therapy. However, the limitations in trial design indicate that these results do not rule out the benefit in carefully selected patients. Evidence from subgroup analyses and non-randomized studies supports invasive endovascular revascularization in presentations such as recurrent flash pulmonary edema, progressive decline in renal function, and hypertension resistant to pharmacologic medical therapy. Endovascular stenting is preferred when anatomy is favorable, while open surgical reconstruction, including aortorenal bypass or endarterectomy, is reserved for complex lesions, failed prior endovascular intervention, or concomitant aortic surgery. The review also discusses emerging strategies, including novel stent platforms and drug-eluting technology, which may improve outcomes if validated in targeted high-risk cohorts.

title: Beta-blocker continuation versus interruption during transcatheter aortic valve implantation: Rationale and design of the BETA-TAVI randomized trial.
authors: Leonidas Koliastasis; Odysseas Katsaros; Charis Armonis; Nikolaos Ktenopoulos; Spyridon Karpathiotakis; Ioannis Doundoulakis; Iro Ntaga; Dimitrios Tsiachris; Sotirios Tsalamandris; Andreas Synetos; Christos Eftychiou; Vlasios Ninios; Athanasios Trikas; Konstantinos Tsioufis; Konstantinos Toutouzas
journal: Cardiovascular revascularization medicine : including molecular interventions
abstract:
Beta-blockers are common in patients referred for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), but there is no consensus on whether they should be continued through the procedure. Continuation could worsen bradycardia or atrioventricular block in a setting already prone to conduction injury, whereas interruption may provoke adrenergic rebound, tachyarrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, or hemodynamic instability. Available evidence is observational and does not resolve this trade-off.
BETA-TAVI is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, open-label, randomized noninferiority trial in adults with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI while receiving chronic oral beta-blocker therapy. Participants are randomized 1:1 to continuation of their usual beta-blocker or interruption from 72 h before TAVI through day 7. The primary endpoint is new permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) within 7 days. Secondary endpoints include high-degree atrioventricular block, new conduction disturbances, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, severe bradycardia, hemodynamic deterioration, mortality, and later PPI. The calculated sample size is 348 participants. The prespecified noninferiority margin is 6.5 percentage points on the absolute risk-difference scale; the primary conclusion requires concordant modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.
BETA-TAVI tests a frequent but poorly studied medication decision using a randomized strategy comparison. The trial will determine whether chronic beta-blocker therapy can be continued through TAVI without a clinically unacceptable increase in early permanent pacing and will characterize the arrhythmic and hemodynamic consequences of both strategies.
gov identifier: NCT05721170.

title: Prompt sensitivity affects large language model decision-making in aortic stenosis: a real-world study of severity classification, treatment recommendation and exploratory prognostic analysis.
authors: Hai-Quan Huang; Shao-Hong Wu; Ying Ban; Cui-Ling Li; Rui Fan; Min Ye; Yan-Qiu Liu; Dong-Hong Liu; Feng-Juan Yao; Wei Li
abstract:
Aortic stenosis (AS) assessment requires integration of discordant echocardiographic and clinical information. The reliability of large language models (LLMs) across prompts and AS phenotypes remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare five LLMs across four prompting strategies for AS severity classification, real-world intervention concordance and exploratory prognostic associations.
This retrospective study evaluated five LLMs across four prompting strategies in 1455 patients with AS. Task 1 assessed AS severity classification and Task 2 assessed real-world intervention concordance. Performance was summarised by accuracy, balanced accuracy and macro-F1. Exploratory associations of the best performing Task 2 configuration with all-cause mortality and heart failure progression were examined using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression.
GPT-o1/chain-of-thought (CoT) achieved the highest Task 1 accuracy (97.53%), balanced accuracy (90.93%) and macro-F1 (83.19%). Grok-2/CoT achieved the highest Task 2 concordance (88.32%). Grok-2/CoT recommendations separated heart failure progression-free survival in unadjusted analysis (p=0.006) but not overall survival (p=0.105). After adjustment, recommendation group was not independently associated with mortality (HR 1.41, 95% CI 0.58 to 3.45, p=0.453) or heart failure progression (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.44 to 2.74, p=0.832).
LLM performance varied by model, task and prompt. Apparent prognostic separation observed in unadjusted analysis was not retained after adjustment for clinical characteristics, AS severity and actual intervention.
LLMs require prompt standardisation, class-specific evaluation and prospective validation before clinical use.

title: First-in-Human Experience With a Novel Monorail Microcatheter for Instantaneous Coronary Pressure and Flow Velocity Measurements.
authors: Alessandro Candreva; Masahiro Hada; Saidamir Djafarov; Gianluca Campo; Divaka Perera; Allen Jeremias; Takuya Mizukami; Bernard De Bruyne; Carlos Collet
abstract:
Invasive coronary physiology enables comprehensive assessment of epicardial and microvascular disease, but its routine use is limited by technical complexity and prolonged acquisition time.
The PyCath system is a rapid-exchange microcatheter engineered to simultaneously measure intracoronary pressure and thermoconvection-based flow velocity.
First-in-human, prospective, single-arm study evaluating the safety and performance of the PyCath system in patients with a clinical indication for coronary physiology assessment. The microcatheter was advanced over a standard coronary guidewire to acquire simultaneous pressure and flow velocity at baseline and during hyperemia. The primary objectives were procedural safety, defined as device-related major adverse cardiac events, and device performance, defined as successful acquisition of pressure and velocity signals. Data were analyzed by an independent core laboratory.
Seventeen patients (mean age 59.3 ± 9.4 years, 76.5% males) referred for invasive coronary physiology assessment were included. Intracoronary pressure and velocity measurements were feasible in 100% and 88% of cases, respectively. The mean time required to obtain both measurements was 70.6 ± 23.6 seconds. The mean fractional flow reserve, coronary flow velocity reserve, and hyperemic microvascular resistance were 0.84 ± 0.12, 2.28 ± 0.79, and 1.46 ± 0.77, respectively. There were no device-related major adverse cardiac events. Test-retest reproducibility was good-to-excellent with intraclass correlation coefficients for fractional flow reserve, coronary flow velocity reserve, and hyperemic microvascular resistance of 0.979 (0.934-0.993), 0.798 (0.477-0.933), and 0.759 (0.397-0.919).
In this first-in-human experience, the PyCath microcatheter enabled safe and reproducible measurements of intracoronary pressure and flow velocity with excellent reproducibility.

title: Right Heart Dysfunction in Valvular Heart Disease: Epidemiology, Prognosis, and Management Considerations.
authors: Michael I Brener; Luigi P Badano; Xavier Galloo; Denisa Muraru; Sean P Pinney; Vallerie V McLaughlin; Jörg Hausleiter; Philip Lurz; Robin Le Ruz; Nicolas M van Mieghem; Ludwig T Weckbach; Gorav Ailawadi; Fabien Praz; Brian R Lindman; Arash Salavitabar; Omar Chehab; Thomas J Stocker; Joann Lindenfeld; Martin B Leon; Daniel Burkhoff; Rebecca T Hahn
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
abstract: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is an important determinant of clinical outcomes across a wide range of cardiovascular pathologies. As the prevalence of valvular heart disease (VHD) increases with the aging population, the intersection between RV function and VHD will become all the more relevant for proper risk assessment, treatment selection, and prognostication. Even though RV dysfunction may not always be attributed to VHD, we aim to give clinicians, researchers, and regulators a deep understanding of how patients with VHD should be evaluated for RV dysfunction and treated when RV dysfunction coexists with VHD. We begin with a discussion of the epidemiology and diagnostic evaluation of RV dysfunction in patients with a variety of VHD subgroups, including right-side (ie, associated with the tricuspid valve) and left-side (ie, associated with the mitral and aortic valves) VHD. Attention is also given in that section to contemporary methods and evolving techniques for identifying and phenotyping different forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD. No single imaging test practically or comprehensively captures all degrees and forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD; therefore, the discussion emphasizes integrating evidence from different imaging modalities and hemodynamic assessments. The second component of the review discusses how RV dysfunction affects therapeutic options, including medical, transcatheter, and surgical therapies for VHD. The focus of the discussion is on the interplay between RV dysfunction in patients with right-side VHD, namely tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Unlike left-side VHD, where RV dysfunction is a marker of overall disease severity but does not necessarily indicate futility or nonresponse to therapy, right-side VHD and TR-associated RV dysfunction identifies a subset of patients where intervention may precipitate even worse RV function. The nuances of these interactions between ventricular and valvular function are the emphasis of this section, and we aim to provide a framework for understanding RV function in the context of these different forms of VHD. Finally, the review concludes with an eye to the future, discussing the ways in which RV dysfunction can be identified and managed with the use of novel techniques. This discussion is increasingly relevant as RV dysfunction and VHD frequently coexist, and accurate identification is critical to matching the right treatment for the right patient.

title: Alfred Kocher technique for prevention of patient-prosthesis mismatch in paediatric patients.
authors: Peter Murin; Martin Winter; Paul Werner; Erhan Urganci; Clemens Atteneder; Alexandra Andreeva; Emilio Osorio-Jaramillo; Daniel Zimpfer; Alfred Kocher
journal: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS
abstract: Aortic valve replacement requires special considerations in paediatric patients, who are not yet fully grown. The Ross procedure remains the gold standard in paediatric patients as it offers growth potential. If the Ross procedure is not feasible, or the size of the aortic annulus precludes placement of an adult-sized mechanical prosthesis, the problem of patient-prosthesis mismatch and subsequent aortic valve reinterventions arises. The standardized option for this patient cohort is the Konno incision and patch ventriculoplasty in combination with an adult-sized mechanical prosthesis, which carries substantial procedural complexity and risk. This video tutorial demonstrates posterior aortic root enlargement using the Alfred Kocher technique in a 7-year-old female with a functionally unicuspid aortic valve and a bicuspid pulmonary valve. The bicuspid pulmonary valve was an unplanned intraoperative finding, making the patient ineligible for a durable autograft transplantation. The technique involves an inverted T-shaped incision in the centre of the non-coronary sinus, and reconstruction with a barrel-shaped patch tailored from a 28 mm Valsalva prosthesis to augment the non-coronary sinus in an anatomical fashion, allowing upsizing by 5 mm in annular diameter. This technique enabled implantation of a 21 mm size mechanical prosthesis (diameter = 24 mm) upsized from a 19 mm annulus.

title: Impact of Computed Tomography-Derived Body Composition on Mortality and Conduction Disturbances After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation: A Sex-Specific Analysis.
authors: Muhammed Rıdvan Ersoysal; Nazmi Kaştan; Batuhan Topcuoğlu; Bahadır Öztürk; Şükriye Uslu; Mustafa Sağan; Nermin Bayar Çakıcı; İclal Erdem Toslak; Şakir Arslan
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is increasingly performed for severe aortic stenosis with improving procedural success rates; however, post-procedural complications remain a significant clinical challenge. Growing evidence suggests that sarcopenia may adversely affect morbidity and mortality in this patient population.
This retrospective, single-center cohort study included 171 patients undergoing elective TAVI (January 2018-February 2024). Muscle area (MA), visceral, subcutaneous (SATA), and total adipose tissue area (TATA) were measured at the L3 vertebral level from pre-procedural computed tomography angiography (CTA). Primary endpoints were all-cause and cardiac mortality; secondary endpoints were permanent cardiac conduction defect, permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI), and hospital stay.
The cohort comprised 95 women (55.5%) and 76 men (44.5%), median age 78.9 years, society of thoracic surgeons score 6.30 (IQR = 4.37-9.33). Over 21.8 ± 17.9 months, 43 patients (25.1%) died, including 12 cardiac deaths (7.0%). Lower MA and MA/body mass index (BMI) ratio were independently associated with cardiac mortality in men (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 0.935, P = .016 and OR = 0.983, P = .042). Permanent cardiac conduction defect occurred in 44 patients (27.7%); lower SATA and TATA were independent predictors in women (OR = 0.990, P = .031 and OR = 0.994, P = .024). Permanent pacemaker implantation was required in 30 patients (18.6%); adipose tissue parameters were associated with PPI in women on univariate analysis but did not retain significance after multiple adjustment.
Pre-procedural CTA-derived body composition assessment may contribute to the prediction of mortality and morbidity in TAVI patients without additional cost or radiation exposure. The association of lower MA with cardiac mortality in men, and of reduced adipose tissue with conduction disturbances in women, suggests that sex-specific body composition parameters may provide prognostic value beyond conventional risk scores.

title: A Murinized Bimagrumab Analogue Increases Skeletal Muscle Mass and Improves Cardiometabolic Remodelling in Experimental Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Tomas Baka; Sophia M Mirrione; Fuzhong Qin; Adam C Gower; Huamei He; Connor Haney; Kuan Ming Su; Simon T Dillon; Towia A Libermann; Kylie Heitman; Andrew P Ryan; Joseph T Brozinick; Francesca Seta; David R Pimentel; Flora Sam; Ivan Luptak
journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
abstract:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) involves left ventricular hypertrophy and metabolic dysfunction. Given the role of skeletal muscle in systemic metabolism, we investigated whether activin type II receptor inhibition with CDD866, a murinized bimagrumab analogue that induces skeletal muscle hypertrophy, improves physical performance and cardiometabolic remodelling in established HCM.
Twenty-four-week-old male mice harbouring the cardiac myosin R403Q mutation received CDD866 or isotype antibody (20 mg/kg subcutaneously every 3 days) for 4 weeks; wild-type (WT) littermates received isotype antibody. Assessments included body composition, muscle imaging and histology, grip strength, treadmill exercise, glucose tolerance, echocardiography, cardiac histopathology, myocardial substrate oxidation by 13C nuclear magnetic resonance in isolated beating hearts and cardiac transcriptomics and proteomics. Values are mean ± SEM.
Compared with R403Q placebo, CDD866 increased lean mass (22.5 ± 0.6 vs. 18.7 ± 0.5 g; p < 0.001), grip strength (135.3 ± 3.4 vs. 99.9 ± 4.3 cN; p < 0.0001) and treadmill distance (99.8 ± 1.7 vs. 77.2 ± 3.2 m; p < 0.0001). Hindlimb muscle volume increased by 24 ± 8% (p < 0.05), and individual muscle weights increased by 44%-87% (all p < 0.0001). CDD866 reduced total left ventricular wall thickness (1.80 ± 0.03 vs. 1.98 ± 0.03 mm; p < 0.001) and improved E/A ratio (1.31 ± 0.04 vs. 0.99 ± 0.04; p < 0.001) and early diastolic mitral annular velocity (18.6 ± 0.7 vs. 14.0 ± 0.7 mm/s; p < 0.01). Cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area and myocardial fibrosis decreased by 32 ± 6% (p < 0.0001) and 69 ± 31% (p < 0.01), respectively. Glucose tolerance was impaired in R403Q mice versus WT (p < 0.01), with a nonsignificant reduction in AUC following CDD866 (p = 0.223). CDD866 increased the fractional contribution of fatty acids to myocardial oxidative metabolism (0.66 ± 0.02 vs. 0.38 ± 0.05; p < 0.01) and reduced 13C-lactate output (15.3 ± 2.5 vs. 40.2 ± 3.8 nmol/min; p < 0.001). Consistent with these measurements, cardiac RNA-seq GSEA showed HCM-associated suppression and CDD866-associated enrichment of fatty acid oxidation, pyruvate metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, ATP synthesis and branched-chain amino acid catabolism (all FDR q < 0.05). Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic upstream regulator predictions provided an exploratory regulatory context for these metabolic findings.
CDD866 increased skeletal muscle mass and performance alongside improvements in cardiac remodelling, diastolic function and myocardial metabolism in established experimental HCM. Activin receptor inhibition offers a promising therapeutic avenue for HCM.

title: Fibrocalcific phenotypes in calcific aortic valve disease: imaging characterization, treatment timing, and efficacy assessment.
authors: Feng Liu; Zhaohong Zeng; Zhian Qian; Wentong Li; Yuting Huang; Ziyou Liu
abstract: Calcific aortic valve disease involves two structural processes, fibrous matrix remodeling and mineral deposition, that contribute unequally between patients, so leaflets of similar hemodynamic severity need not share the same tissue composition. Histologic and multi-omics studies have mapped this heterogeneity across sex, age, and valve morphology, and contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography (CTA) has brought compositional assessment into living patients and into longitudinal follow-up. Calcific burden behaves consistently: it tracks stenosis severity, predicts progression, and carries prognostic weight. Findings for noncalcified tissue are less settled and depend on the population studied and on how the measurement is made. Whether total fibrocalcific volume performs well as a structural endpoint and whether CTA-derived noncalcified tissue volume adds predictive value beyond calcification are consequently two separate questions, and the literature often merges them. Pharmacologic trials in patients have almost always measured calcification progression or hemodynamics rather than longitudinal change in the fibrous matrix. Randomized lipid-lowering and mineral-targeted trials in patients have been negative, whereas animal and cell experiments show that established mineral lesions, cell states, and function can sometimes be modified, although these responses do not necessarily move together. This review integrates histology, multimodality imaging, clinical cohorts, pharmacologic trials, and preclinical intervention studies to define the fibrocalcific phenotype, distinguish prevention from slowing and reversal, and align therapeutic timing with endpoints at the levels of activity, tissue burden, valve function, myocardial response, and clinical events. Longitudinal measurement of leaflet composition and validation of treatment-induced change against functional outcomes remain the central gaps.

title: Elevated Serum Growth Differentiation Factor 15 Levels Predict Poor Prognosis in Patients With Aortic Stenosis Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation.
authors: Shunsuke Edamura; Harutoshi Tamura; Yoichiro Otaki; Atsushi Iizuka; Tomoki Kobayashi; Takayuki Sugai; Masahiro Wanezaki; Satoshi Nishiyama; Naoaki Hashimoto; Daisuke Kinoshita; Shigehiko Kato; Takanori Arimoto; Tetsu Watanabe; Masafumi Watanabe
abstract:
Despite transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) reducing cardiovascular events in elderly patients with aortic stenosis (AS), the mortality rate is still high. Growth differentiation factor (GDF) 15 is reportedly a useful prognostic marker for clinical outcomes in the field of cardiovascular diseases, but it is still unclear if elevated serum GDF15 levels predict poor prognosis in patients with severe AS who undergo TAVI.
We measured the pre- and postoperative serum concentrations of GDF15 in 148 patients. The primary and secondary endpoints were all-cause death and a composite event including cardiovascular death, heart failure rehospitalization, stroke, and adverse bleeding event, respectively. There were 30 all-cause deaths and 21 composite events during a median follow-up period of 1,023 days. Both pre- and postoperative serum GDF15 levels were significantly increased with advancing Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality score. Multivariate Cox proportional hazards analysis revealed that preoperative serum GDF15 level was independently associated with the primary and secondary endpoints, and the postoperative serum GDF15 level was independently associated with the primary endpoint after adjustment for confounding risk factors. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis for the primary endpoint showed a comparable area under the curve for the pre- and postoperative serum GDF15 levels.
Both the pre- and postoperative GDF15 concentration could be a feasible marker for clinical outcomes in Japanese patients undergoing TAVI.

title: Prognostic Implications of Clinically Attributed Left Atrial Enlargement Subtypes in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation.
authors: Tatsuya Sato; Asahiro Ito; Yuki Kitagawa; Shinji Ito; Hiroki Yamaura; Akihiro Okamoto; Nanaka Nomura; Tomohiro Yamaguchi; Shunsuke Kagawa; Mana Ogawa; Takenobu Shimada; Sera Ishikawa; Yusuke Hayashi; Atsushi Shibata; Kenichiro Otsuka; Daiju Fukuda
abstract:
Left atrial enlargement (LAE) is common in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), but its prognostic significance may vary according to the clinical drivers of atrial remodeling. We examined whether prognostic factors differ by clinically attributed LAE subtype in patients undergoing TAVI with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF).
We retrospectively analyzed 317 consecutive patients with symptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AS) undergoing TAVI who had preserved LVEF and LAE. Patients were classified as AS-associated LAE (no atrial fibrillation [AF] and <moderate mitral regurgitation [MR]) or AF/MR-associated LAE (AF and/or ≥moderate MR). The primary endpoint was all-cause death. During a median follow-up of 2.7 years, 69 patients (21.8%) died. The all-cause mortality rate was higher in the AF/MR-associated group than in the AS-associated LAE group (30.7% vs. 19.0%; log-rank P<0.01), but this association was attenuated after adjustment for eGFR, log-BNP, and LAVI. In the AS-associated LAE group, higher log-BNP (hazard ratio (HR) 1.45, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.06-1.98), higher E/e' (HR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01-1.06), and lower TAPSE (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81-0.99) predicted death. In the AF/MR-associated LAE group, lower eGFR (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.93-1.00) and higher log-BNP (HR 1.98, 95% CI 1.09-3.59) predicted death after adjustment for age. Interactions were significant for eGFR and E/e'.
Prognostic markers after TAVI differ by clinically attributed LAE subtype, supporting subtype-informed risk stratification.

title: Electrical Storm Triggered by Conus Branch Occlusion During Elective Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Very Severe Aortic Stenosis: Rescue With Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty Under Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
authors: Taiki Kodama; Nobuhiro Honda; Saya Hiromatsu; Seigo Masuda
journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions
abstract: We report a case of very severe aortic stenosis (AS) in which side-branch occlusion during elective percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) precipitated life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and hemodynamic collapse. The patient was a 72-year-old man with very severe AS who was scheduled to undergo a valve intervention. Preprocedural coronary angiography revealed a significant, newly developed stenosis in the right coronary artery, and an elective PCI was performed prior to valve treatment. Following intravascular lithotripsy and drug-eluting stent implantation, occlusion of the conus branch occurred, triggering recurrent ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Despite initiation of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and intra-aortic balloon pump support, the patient's hemodynamic status did not improve. Because excessive afterload due to very severe AS was considered the principal pathophysiological mechanism, emergency balloon aortic valvuloplasty was performed. This resulted in rapid hemodynamic stabilization and complete resolution of ventricular arrhythmias. This case illustrates that even a minor side-branch occlusion during PCI can lead to catastrophic outcomes in patients with very severe AS. Furthermore, it highlights that mechanical circulatory support alone may be insufficient, and that prompt relief of valvular obstruction is essential. Careful consideration of the indications and sequence of coronary intervention through discussions with a heart team is warranted for patients with very severe AS.

title: Genetically predicted lipoprotein(a), first and recurrent venous thromboembolism, and coagulation proteins: evidence against causal relationships.
authors: Iyas Daghlas; Dipender Gill
abstract: Lipoprotein(a) exhibits in vitro antifibrinolytic properties, though it remains uncertain whether this translates into an effect on thromboembolic disease risk. We applied Mendelian randomization (MR) to evaluate the relationship between genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) levels, venous thromboembolism (VTE), and circulating coagulation protein levels. We instrumented lipoprotein(a) using two genetic variants (rs10455872 and rs3798220) that explain 36% of circulating lipoprotein(a) variance. The primary outcomes were first (81,190 cases) and recurrent VTE (1,775 cases). Comparator outcomes included coronary artery disease (181,522 cases) and calcific aortic stenosis (13,765 cases). We performed MR analyses to estimate the association of a genetically predicted 100 nmol/L increase in lipoprotein(a) with each outcome. In exploratory analyses, we tested associations with levels of 35 coagulation proteins in the UK Biobank (n = 46,218) and deCODE (n = 35,559) cohorts. Genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) was associated with a small reduction in risk of first VTE (odds ratio [OR] 0.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96-0.99, P = 0.002), though this was not supported by colocalization (posterior=12%), suggesting that the MR association was driven by genetic confounding. There was no association with recurrent VTE (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.91-1.16, P = 0.68). In contrast, genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) was strongly associated with increased risk of coronary artery disease (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.29-1.33) and calcific aortic stenosis (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.30-1.40). After multiple testing correction, genetically predicted lipoprotein(a) had no significant association with any coagulation proteins. Human genetic evidence does not support a clinically meaningful role for lipoprotein(a) in VTE risk. These findings support targeting of lipoprotein(a)-lowering therapies toward atherosclerotic and valvular diseases rather than thromboembolic indications.

title: Artificial Intelligence‒Guided Phenotyping of Cardiomyopathies: From Detection to Surveillance.
authors: Evangelos K Oikonomou; Rohan Khera; Ahmad Masri
abstract: The management of cardiomyopathies relies on timely diagnosis, precise phenotyping, multimodal risk stratification, and longitudinal monitoring. These tasks require integration of high-dimensional signals from patient history, electrocardiography, imaging, biomarkers, and longitudinal health records, data streams well-suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled pattern recognition and prediction. Among inherited and acquired cardiomyopathies, hypertrophic (HCM) and transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) best exemplify this opportunity. Both remain systematically underdiagnosed, span a continuous phenotypic spectrum, and are increasingly actionable through disease-modifying therapies. Emerging AI approaches applied to multimodality data streams can identify latent disease, quantify its severity, and predict its trajectory. Beyond diagnosis, AI paves the path for opportunistic screening, longitudinal surveillance, risk stratification, and novel clinical trial designs. Realizing this promise requires careful attention to label quality, generalizability, false-positive burden in low-prevalence settings, and prospective evidence that the human-AI synergy improves outcomes. In this review, we use HCM and ATTR-CM as key examples to synthesize the current evidence of AI in cardiomyopathies and propose a forward-looking framework for AI-guided disease phenotyping, with emphasis on regulation, implementation, and clinical evaluation.

title: Intelligent energy management of a novel non-isolated bidirectional dual-input single-output converter for electric vehicle applications.
authors: Faridha Banu M R; Jayapragash R
abstract: For use in electric vehicle (EV) applications, this paper suggests a non-isolated bidirectional Dual-Input Single-Output (DISO) DC-DC converter with an intelligent energy management method. The proposed converter integrates photovoltaic (PV) and battery energy sources in a single power conversion structure, which results in fewer components, higher efficiency and bidirectional power flow capability. The converter is designed based on a two-phase interleaved boost topology with a relay-assisted reconfiguration stage that facilitates flexible source selection, battery charging/discharging and regenerative braking operation. A Modified Deep Neural Network (MODNN) based intelligent energy management strategy is proposed to enhance energy utilization and adaptive power sharing. The proposed MODNN modifies a conventional single-task feedforward DNN by introducing a shared-trunk, multi-head architecture that jointly predicts the discrete operating mode and the continuous converter duty ratios through a composite classification-regression loss function, benchmarked against recent machine-learning baselines (k-NN, a bagged neural-network ensemble, and LSTM) under identical training/test conditions. In the proposed MODNN framework, the PV voltage, PV current, battery state-of-charge, battery voltage, and load demand information are used to decide the optimal operating mode and power flow condition under different operating scenarios. The converter provides flexible power distribution between available energy sources, productive use of regenerative braking energy, uninterrupted load supply and effective battery management. The performance of the proposed converter is verified by MATLAB/Simulink simulations, and the converter topology is experimentally validated with a laboratory prototype of 500 W. The experimental results show that the five operating modes operate successfully with a peak efficiency of 96.7%, which validates the effectiveness of the proposed converter for EV energy management applications.

title: Dynamic scale fusion and cascaded prototype refinement for few-shot sports image classification.
authors: Dongfang Gao; Yuyan Ruan; Chun Chang; Wenzhu Yao
abstract:
Sports image classification plays a crucial role in intelligent sports analytics by supporting athlete behavior analysis, training feedback, exercise participation monitoring, and data-driven sports behavior studies. Although deep learning methods have advanced sports image recognition by learning hierarchical visual patterns from image data, they usually require abundant annotations, which limits their applicability in few-shot scenarios. In addition, sports images often show large-scale variations, severe background distraction, and fine-grained inter-class similarities, further degrading recognition performance under scarce supervision.
To address these challenges, this study proposes a dynamic scale fusion and cascaded prototype refinement network (DSCPNet) for few-shot sports image classification. First, Dynamic Scale Fusion Attention (DSFA) is introduced to dynamically select and fuse discriminative contextual cues under varying receptive fields, thereby enhancing scale-adaptive feature representation from scarce support samples. Second, Cascaded Foreground-Scene Interaction (CFSI) is designed to suppress background interference through cascaded interaction modulation, strengthening target-focused embeddings and reducing intra-class variance. Finally, Cross-Prototype Feature Refinement (CPFR) is developed to calibrate support prototypes and query representations in a cross-prototype manner, producing more discriminative class prototypes and improving the robustness of similarity estimation for fine-grained recognition.
Experiments on two sports-oriented few-shot benchmark datasets show that DSCPNet consistently achieves stronger recognition performance than competing methods in both 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios.
These results indicate that DSCPNet can improve few-shot sports image recognition under scale variation, background distraction, and fine-grained inter-class ambiguity. The proposed framework provides an effective solution for sports image classification when labeled samples are limited.

title: Toward trustworthy diagnostic AI: debiasing and grounding large language models for seizure semiology interpretation.
authors: Xiaolei Yuan; Xinyue Zhang; Hui Xu; Qing Ye; Canxing Yuan; Hui Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed to map free-text seizure semiology to seizure-onset-zone (SOZ) likelihoods, but it remains unclear whether inference-time interventions can improve on the original SemioLLM benchmark without additional training. We evaluated two such interventions, candidate-order permutation within self-consistency and TF-IDF retrieval of case-specific labelled examples, individually and in combination (retrieval-augmented order-invariant self-consistency, RAOI-SC), across seven locally served open-weight LLMs on 1,268 Semio2Brain rows. Performance was assessed with weighted- and macro-F1, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and exact McNemar tests against the self-consistency baseline, and a multi-dimensional reliability profile covering citation coverage and conditional verifiability, retrieval agreement, strict schema adherence, and confidence concentration; a TF-IDF nearest-neighbor classifier and grouped-split sensitivity analyses bounded how much of any gain could reflect retrieval leakage rather than the intervention itself. RAOI-SC had a higher weighted-F1 point estimate than self-consistency for six of seven models, but the improvement was supported by paired confidence intervals for four models and by McNemar testing for only one, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3; the TF-IDF nearest-neighbor baseline alone achieved 55.72 weighted-F1 under row-level splitting, falling to 50.43 and 48.97 once identical-text and publication-reference duplicates were grouped together. These results support a cautious, model-specific reading of retrieval and order permutation as testable prompting interventions rather than a universally superior or clinically validated method, and define a row-level benchmark that does not by itself establish patient- or source-level generalization.

title: Understanding the Inner Workings of Large Language Models in Medicine.
authors: Georg Fuellen; Hans Jarchow; Johann-Christian Põder
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly influencing medical practice, education, and research. Their responsible integration into healthcare requires expertise in medical, ethical, practical, and theoretical domains.
We prompted GPT-o1 to generate examples illustrating how understanding transformer architecture can facilitate output interpretation. Key topics were extracted from its responses, and illustrative cases were identified and cross-checked against the peer-reviewed literature using Consensus.app, an AI-assisted literature-search tool.
Five key topics were identified: (1) anticipating contextual focus in medical reasoning, (2) explaining "generic" or "textbook" responses, (3) understanding strengths and weaknesses in differential diagnosis, (4) explaining ambiguous or contradictory responses, and (5) identifying hallucinations in unfamiliar scenarios. Case examples highlight both benefits and limitations, including accurate attention to salient clinical details, reliance on generalized patterns, risks of base rate neglect in differential diagnosis, challenges of ambiguous prompts, and hallucinations in rare or underrepresented cases.
A theoretical understanding of LLMs is crucial for responsible clinical integration. Distinguishing between well-represented (short head) and underrepresented (long tail) knowledge, recognizing generic responses, and identifying hallucinations are essential competencies. Coupled with medical and ethical expertise, these skills will enable healthcare professionals to leverage LLMs effectively while mitigating risks.

title: PixelVision: A Modular Web-Based Framework for AI-Assisted Biological Image Analysis Across Diverse Microscopy Modalities.
authors: Arpit Tandon; Ayse B Oktay; Eric McAfee; Adrian J Green; Brian E Howard; Mihir Shah; Ruchir R Shah
abstract: The increasing volume and heterogeneity of microscopy data in biomedical research present challenges for automated image analysis and the integration of assay-specific computational methods. We developed PixelVision, a modular, web-based framework that integrates deep learning models, quantitative image analysis, and expert review across diverse biological imaging modalities. The framework supports single-organism imaging, two- and three-dimensional cell culture analysis, whole-slide imaging, and interactive annotation through a shared infrastructure for model deployment, version management, and data processing. Quantitative evaluations demonstrated application-specific classification and segmentation performance, with inference throughput of approximately seven high-resolution images per second on a single GPU. In a prospective zebrafish screening study, iterative model refinement using expert-reviewed classifications was associated with an increase in macro-averaged F1 score from 0.867 to 0.967 across three screening rounds. PixelVision provides a framework for integrating automated image analysis and expert assessment across heterogeneous microscopy workflows.

title: Surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search for antimicrobial peptide sequence optimization and in vitro antibacterial assessment.
authors: Jang-Jih Lu; Chia-Ru Chung; Chen-Hao Chang; Li-Ching Wu; Justin Bo-Kai Hsu; Cheng-Yu Tsai; Tzong-Yi Lee; Jorng-Tzong Horng
abstract: The rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens necessitates the development of novel therapeutic agents, yet the de novo design of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) is challenged by the vast combinatorial search space and the difficulty of balancing efficacy with toxicity. To address these limitations, we introduce a reinforcement learning framework that employs surrogate-guided self-play Monte Carlo tree search to explore the peptide landscape. By integrating surrogate models for predicted antimicrobial activity, HemoDL-predicted hemolytic propensity, and ESMFold structural confidence, the system performs multi-property computational optimization and candidate prioritization. In silico analysis demonstrated that the optimized peptides adopt amphipathic α-helical structures with high predicted folding confidence and possess favorable docking scores against Staphylococcus aureus resistance targets, including PBP2a and MurA. To assess the biological relevance of the computationally prioritized candidates, 16 peptides were synthesized and evaluated by agar dilution against a 37-strain bacterial panel over a concentration range of 0.25-64 μg/ml. AMP2, AMP7, and AMP9 achieved complete inhibition of at least one tested strain, corresponding to 3 of 16 synthesized candidates (18.75%). AMP12 and AMP13 showed partial growth reduction without complete inhibition within the tested range, whereas the remaining 11 candidates showed no complete inhibition. These findings quantify the current gap between surrogate-defined computational enrichment and assay-specific antibacterial activity. The strain-dependent experimental outcomes further indicate that surrogate, docking, and structural scores do not fully capture all determinants of antibacterial efficacy. The experimental assessment was limited to bacterial agar-dilution activity; mammalian-cell cytotoxicity, wet-lab hemolysis, and peptide-stability assays were not performed. In conclusion, this study establishes a computational framework for the design of bioactive peptides and provides structural insights for bridging the gap between deep learning predictions and experimental outcomes.

title: Machine learning-based experimental access to photon-by-photon arrival times in scintillation detectors.
authors: Yuya Onishi; Ryosuke Ota; Fumio Hashimoto; Kibo Ote; Go Akamatsu; Hideaki Tashima; Taiga Yamaya
abstract: Objective. Scintillation detectors with excellent timing resolution enable more precise localization of radiation sources in positron emission tomography, leading to substantial improvements in diagnostic capability for diseases such as cancer and dementia. At the timing precision required for such applications at the picosecond scale, detector performance is governed by the dynamics of scintillation photons generated within the detector and their subsequent detection processes. However, detector signals have conventionally been treated only as collective responses of many photons due to structural constraints inherent to photodetectors. In this study, we overcome this fundamental limitation using deep learning framework.Approach. The proposed method estimates photon-by-photon arrival times directly from detector waveforms without requiring any modification to the detector structure; the method operates on an event-by-event basis without ground-truth labels by integrating an unsupervised learning framework with a physically informed detector-response model.Main results. Through comprehensive validation combining Monte Carlo simulation and experimental measurements across various detector configurations, we experimentally demonstrate improved timing resolution, visualized depth-of-interaction-dependent photon transport, and classified Cherenkov and scintillation photons based on the estimated photon-level timing information using a unified deep learning-based framework.Significance. These results provide experimental access to photon dynamics, bridging the gap between theoretical modeling and experimental observation, and they open a new data-driven pathway for discovery in detector physics and optimization.

title: A Topology-Feature Disentangled Deep Clustering Method for scRNA-seq Based on Graph-to-MLP Distillation.
authors: Xilai Gao; Hao Liu; Yang Zhao; Xiaoyi Lv; Xiangwei Zhao; Cheng Chen
abstract:
Graph neural networks (GNNs), owing to their ability to model topological relationships between cells, have gradually emerged as a mainstream approach in the clustering analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. However, their practical application still faces the following challenges: (1) excessive smoothing undermines cellular heterogeneity; (2) pre-constructed graphs introduce end-to-end dependencies; (3) large-scale cellular graph computations are computationally intensive.
To fully utilise the expression profiles and topological information contained within scRNA-seq data and overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a Graph-to-MLP (G2M) knowledge distillation method incorporating AdaBoost principles, and builds upon this to develop a graph-disentangled single-cell clustering framework-scAdaG2M. This framework utilises a GNN teacher model to learn higher-order topological relationships and local neighbourhood structures between cells on a cellular graph, whilst multiple lightweight MLP student models perform feature learning in an ungraphed setting. By combining this with an AdaBoost-style dynamic reweighting strategy, the framework enhances the model's ability to characterise cells that are difficult to distinguish, cells with blurred boundaries, and potentially rare cell populations, thereby mitigating the dilution of cellular heterogeneity caused by over-smoothing. At the same time, this framework effectively decouples graph-based modelling from graph-free reasoning, reduces the end-to-end reliance on pre-constructed graphs, and significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with large-scale cellular graphs.
All datasets used in this study are publicly available. Detailed information about all the single-cell datasets analyzed in this paper is provided in Supplementary Table 1. The source code is available at https://github.com/gxl1110/scAdaG2M and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21512950.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Enhancing Cone-Beam Computed Tomography Image Quality Using Deep Learning-based Super-Resolution.
authors: Hossein Mohammad-Rahimi; Ali Nosrat; Lars Schropp; Jennifer Christensen; Matheus Sampaio-Oliveira; Rubens Spin-Neto; Ruben Pauwels
abstract:
To develop deep learning super-resolution (SR) models for enhancing cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT).
Seventy CBCT volumes (75 µm voxel size) served as references. Paired low-resolution (LR) volumes (300 µm) were simulated using physics-based degradation. Four architectures were each trained with three loss configurations (L1; L1+edge; L1+edge+perceptual): Swin Transformer for Image Restoration (SwinIR), Hybrid Attention Transformer (HAT), Hybrid Multi-Axis Aggregation Network (HMA-Net), and Dense-Residual-Connected Transformer (DRCT). Performance was assessed with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and deep image structure and texture similarity (DISTS). Three dentists ranked the 12 configurations in 28 sets using blinded forced-choice pairwise comparisons. Correlations of metrics and expert ranks were assessed using Spearman correlation.
All configurations outperformed LR input and bicubic interpolation on every metric (p < 0.05). HMA-Net trained with L1+edge+perceptual loss performed best on LPIPS (0.216) and DISTS (0.186). HAT with L1 loss achieved the highest PSNR (28.79 dB) and SSIM (0.820). Experts ranked DRCT and HAT with L1 loss, and DRCT with L1+edge loss, as the best configurations (p < 0.001 versus others). Expert rank correlated moderately only with PSNR (rho = -0.65) and SSIM (rho = -0.60; both p < 0.05).
Transformer-based SR improved the perceived quality of clinical CBCT images. HAT and DRCT trained with L1 pixel loss alone, and DRCT trained with L1 and edge loss, demonstrated superior performance.
Transformer-based super-resolution improved expert-perceived detail of simulated low-resolution in vivo CBCT scans without additional radiation dose, supporting further validation on directly acquired low-resolution scans.

title: EXPRESS: Blood-free full quantification of dynamic TSPO PET imaging with [11C]PBR28.
authors: Ludovica Brusaferri; Alexander C Whitehead; Leonardo Barzon; Lucia Maccioni; Zeynab Alshelh; Minhae Kim; Antonio Micoli; Nicola Toschi; Matteo Ferrante; Marianna Inglese; Ciprian Catana; Jodi Gilman; Mattia Veronese; Oliver D Howes; Tiago Marques; Maria Antonietta Nettis; Valeria Mondelli; Carmine M Pariante; Federico E Turkheimer; Enrico Grisan; Marco Loggia
journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
abstract:
Quantitative dynamic PET imaging requires metabolite-corrected arterial input functions, traditionally obtained through invasive arterial blood sampling, limiting broader adoption of quantitative kinetic modelling. Achieving generalisability across datasets, scanners, and imaging centres remains a major challenge for data-driven alternatives.
We developed ASTRA, a deep-learning-based framework for arterial input function estimation from dynamic brain TSPO PET. ASTRA was developed and validated using arterial measurements in one dataset (n=90), then transfer-learned and evaluated against arterial measurements at a second centre (n=52). Building upon this, ASTRA was applied to an independent clinical cohort (n=32) from the second site but without arterial reference data, where quantitative analyses had therefore not been performed, to assess whether it could reproduce previously reported semi-quantitative cross-sectional group differences. Robustness to altered tracer kinetics was evaluated in an out-of-distribution pharmacological blockade cohort (n=5).
ASTRA-derived quantitative estimates agreed with arterial measurements (VT: CCC=0.658-0.805), with higher uncertainty associated with greater error. In the clinical cohort, ASTRA reproduced SUVR-based group differences using DVR (p<0.001), except in the pituitary gland (p=0.12). Finally, ASTRA yielded receptor occupancy estimates (0.92±0.17) closely matching arterial values (0.94±0.12) in the blocking cohort.
These findings demonstrate the feasibility of multi-site, non-invasive quantitative TSPO PET.

title: Human-AI interaction in parotid ultrasound diagnosis: a prospective two-phase observer-performance study.
authors: Jeonghwan Kim; Seyeon Lee; Hyewon Hwang; Soonho Ha; Yeongmin Kim; Inyong Jeong; Min-Suk Kim; Byungjae Kang; Joon Hong Kim; Sung Jun Hong; Young Hen Lee; Yeon Soo Kim; Seung-Kuk Baek; Sung-Hye You; Hyojeong Kim; Hyun Soo Park; Yeojin Yoo; Thomas J Kwack; Soon Young Kwon; Hwamin Lee
abstract:
Differentiating pleomorphic adenoma (PA) from Warthin's tumor (WT) - the two most common benign parotid neoplasms - on ultrasound is challenging even for experienced ultrasonographers. Most existing AI systems for parotid ultrasound have been static, retrospective, and tested without prospective reader evaluation. We developed a confidence-aware AI system with a radiologist-editable interface and prospectively evaluated its impact on radiologist performance in an observer-performance study.
We developed a confidence-aware hybrid pipeline combining a YOLO detection model with a classification model fallback for parotid ultrasound differentiation, using an internal dataset of 949 images (Korea University Ansan Hospital) and an external dataset of 427 images (Korea University Anam Hospital). We exploratorily evaluated 35 detection × classification combinations to characterize model complementarity, and then prospectively validated a single pre-specified deployment configuration (τ = 0.80, YOLOv12m + ConvNeXt) through a two-phase observer-performance study with three board-certified radiologists on 107 external cases (321 reads total).
Standalone detection and classification models achieved external AUROCs of 0.811 and 0.919, respectively. The confidence-aware pipeline outperformed both standalone models in 22 of 35 combinations on external data (highest macro-F1 = 0.838) with the complementary effect most apparent when the two models performed comparably. In the reader study, AI assistance improved pooled diagnostic accuracy from 76.3% to 81.6% (generalized linear mixed model [GLMM] odds ratio = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12-2.13, p = 0.008) and inter-reader agreement (Fleiss' κ increasing from 0.475 to 0.611), with larger gains on more difficult cases. Reader response was selective: readers followed correct AI predictions more often than incorrect ones (76.2% vs. 51.1%, p = 0.008), and per-class sensitivity changed in opposite directions for WT (+ 18.1% points) and PA (- 9.3% points), aligning with the AI's prediction profile.
A confidence-aware AI system with a radiologist-editable interface improved radiologist diagnostic accuracy and inter-reader agreement in a prospective observer-performance study. These findings support the system's potential as a decision-support tool that operates alongside the interpreting physician, and motivate further evaluation in real-world clinical workflows.

title: Performance of large language models in the management of all types of dental trauma: a comprehensive evaluation of IADT guideline adherence, communicative quality, and readability.
authors: Beyhan Başkan; Nilgün Bulut; Hatice Kübra Başkan
abstract:
This study comparatively evaluated the clinical decision support capacity of four large language models (LLMs) in dental trauma management, assessing the International Association of Dental Traumatology (IADT) guideline adherence as the primary outcome and communicative quality and readability as secondary outcomes.
Thirty-six clinical scenarios covering all trauma types in primary and permanent dentition were developed based on IADT 2024 guidelines and submitted to four LLMs using a standardized prompt. IADT guideline adherence was evaluated with the Dental Trauma Clinical Reliability and Guideline Adherence Index (DeTra-GAI), a 20-item rubric covering five clinical domains (maximum score: 40). Communicative quality was assessed using DISCERN, EQIP, and GQS scales, and readability was evaluated using FRE, FKGL, GFI, and SMOG indices. Two independent experts performed blinded scoring. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis tests, two-way ART ANOVA, and Spearman correlations.
Significant performance differences were observed among models (p = 0.026). ChatGPT-5.1 achieved the highest IADT Compliance Score (39.67 ± 0.99), followed by Gemini 2.5 Pro (39.00 ± 2.48), Claude 4.5 (38.69 ± 1.98), and Grok 4.1 (35.22 ± 9.17). Grok 4.1 showed significantly lower performance in Emergency Management and Patient Safety domains (p < 0.001) but scored higher in DISCERN and EQIP transparency dimensions. ChatGPT-5.1 achieved the highest GQS (4.14 ± 0.87) while producing the least readable content (FRE: 23.67); Claude 4.5 demonstrated relatively better readability (SMOG: 7.7 ± 0.39). Trauma type significantly affected all metrics (p < 0.001), and dentition stage influenced GQS scores (p = 0.003).
Although LLMs demonstrate substantial alignment with IADT guidelines, communicative clarity, source transparency, and readability vary significantly across models. The primary limitation lies not in clinical accuracy but in insufficient clarity for emergency workflows. Findings should be interpreted within the constraints of text-based scenarios, and clinical decisions must remain under professional oversight.

title: A 9 + 1 multi-agent collaborative teaching model for clinical reasoning: integrating large language models into medical education.
authors: Qian Dong; Jing Chang; Cheng Zhang; Jing Wu; Panpan Feng; Rui Feng; Guoli Yang; Min Mao
abstract:
Clinical reasoning-the cognitive and metacognitive processes through which clinicians collect and interpret patient information, generate and test diagnostic hypotheses, and make clinical decisions-is a core competency in medical education. Since 1956, clinical educators have innovated methods to build this key skill. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, especially large language models (LLMs), have advanced rapidly. For example, OpenAI's inaugural LLM scored 96.5% on the Medical Question Answering (MedQA) benchmark, rivaling top human performers. Integrating AI into teaching prompts key questions: Can it support students' clinical reasoning development? This requires careful investigation.
Guided by the Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation (ADDIE) instructional design model and Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology, this study explored approaches for fostering clinical reasoning through LLM integration. We traced the educational evolution of clinical reasoning since 1956 and identified five core competencies: organizing knowledge structures, reasoning and judgment, cognitive regulation, communication and collaboration, and self-development. Building on these findings, we designed a "9 + 1" multi-agent collaborative teaching model covering an end-to-end closed-loop training process from instructional design to reflective feedback. We conducted a preliminary A/B controlled experiment comparing traditional methods (Group A, n = 30) with the 9 + 1 model (Group B, n = 30). Learning outcomes were assessed using a Mini-Objective Structured Clinical Examination (Mini-OSCE) tool.
In the "chest pain case" experiment, Group B students showed marked gains in hypothesis completeness, cognitive error spotting, and reflection depth compared to Group A. These differences were statistically significant.
Our "9 + 1" model enables collaborative engagement among teachers, students, and AI agents within Team-Based Learning (TBL) scenarios. Preliminary findings suggest it may help students develop knowledge structures and critical thinking in a more structured manner, while allowing teachers to identify challenging learning modules and offer targeted support. This approach shows potential for broader application in clinical education, though further validation with larger samples and diverse settings is needed.

title: How reliable are large language models in pediatric dentistry? Performance of seven artificial intelligence models on dental specialty examination questions (2012-2024).
authors: Hüsniye Gümüş; Gülce Öztürk; Aybüke Bahadır Sezer
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used in dental education; however, their reliability in the field of pediatric dentistry remains unclear. This study aimed to compare the accuracy rates of seven different LLMs in answering pediatric dentistry questions from the Turkish Dental Specialty Examination (DSE).
A cross-sectional evaluation was conducted on a total of 174 multiple-choice pediatric dentistry questions derived from 18 DSE administered between 2012 and 2024. The questions were categorized into 13 subdomains and further classified as clinical/case-based or theoretical/knowledge-based. The performance of seven different LLMs (ChatGPT-4.1 Pro, ChatGPT-5 Pro, Claude Pro, Copilot Pro, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini Advanced 2.5 Experimental, and Perplexity Pro) was assessed. Accuracy rates were compared across models, subdomains, and question types, and factors predicting correct responses were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.
Accuracy rates differed significantly among the models (p = 0.019). The highest accuracy was observed with Gemini Advanced 2.5 Experimental (93.7%), whereas the lowest was with Claude Pro (82.8%). Accuracy rates also varied significantly across subdomains (p < 0.001), with lower performance observed in Restorative treatments/materials (75.5%) and Fluoride/preventive applications (78.6%). Clinical questions were answered with higher accuracy than theoretical questions (93.7% vs. 86.2%). In the regression analysis, the Gemini Advanced 2.5 Experimental model and clinical question type were identified as independent predictors of correct responses compared with ChatGPT-5 Pro.
LLMs demonstrated high performance in answering pediatric dentistry questions derived from the Turkish DSE; however, these findings should be interpreted in light of the standardized, examination-based nature of the assessment. LLMs should be used as complementary tools in pediatric dentistry education and similar domain-specific educational contexts, rather than as substitutes for expert clinical judgment.

title: Deep learning model for automatic detection of incidental adrenal abnormalities on low-dose computed tomography images.
authors: Kexin Wang; He Wang; Shiwei Chen; Wencong Han; Wenzhi Gao; Guangyong Shi; Tong Liu; Chongchen Ma; Jiangtao Liu; Xiangpeng Wang; Zheng Zhang
abstract:
To investigate the feasibility of employing deep learning models for automated segmentation and classification of adrenal incidental abnormalities on low-dose CT images.
Four distinct CT cohorts were retrospectively collected for deep learning models development (cohort A, n = 2574; cohort B, n = 1205), internal evaluation (cohort C, n = 3681), and external evaluation (cohort D, n = 779). Two experienced uroradiologists independently reviewed the CT images and labeled the adrenal glands as normal or abnormal based on predefined criteria encompassing both density and morphological abnormalities, with any discrepancies resolved through consultation. The model development cohorts were divided into a training set, a validation set, and a test set. Deep learning models for segmentation and classification were trained and evaluated on internal and external sets, with the dice similarity coefficient (DSC), area under precision-recall curves (AUPRC), and area under receiver operating characteristic curves (AUROC) as evaluation metrics. Adrenal descriptions from radiology reports were extracted to compare with the model's performance.
For adrenal gland segmentation, the DSC values for the test set, internal validation cohort, and external validation cohort were 0.839 (IQR: 0.783-0.871), 0.870 (IQR: 0.819-0.902), and 0.799 (IQR: 0.729-0.849), respectively. For adrenal gland classification, the AI model achieved AUPRC values of 0.913, 0.753, and 0.927 in the test set, internal validation cohort, and external validation cohort, respectively, outperforming routine radiology reporting (AUPRC: 0.809, 0.708, 0.591; all P < 0.05). Corresponding AUROC values were 0.956, 0.942, and 0.977 for the AI model, which also outperformed routine radiology reporting (AUROC: 0.889, 0.705, 0.551; all P < 0.05).
The deep learning models showed promise in automated adrenal segmentation and classification, highlighting AI's potential to improve detection of adrenal abnormalities in LDCT scans.
This study has been registered on ClinicalTrials.gov on August 25, 2025, with the unique identifier NCT07198152.

title: AI as gatekeeper: a cross-sectional study of AI-generated peer review of landmark oncological studies.
authors: Efe Cem Erdat; Güngör Utkan
abstract:
The increasing volume of scientific manuscripts has strained traditional peer-review systems, prompting interest in artificial intelligence (AI) as a potential solution. However, the comparative performance of large language models (LLMs) in critically appraising oncological research remains unexplored.
We conducted a cross-sectional study evaluating the peer-review capabilities of three LLMs-Claude Sonnet 4.5, Google Gemini 3.0 Thinking, and OpenAI ChatGPT 5.1-using 50 blinded landmark oncology trials identified from ASCO, ESMO, and NCCN guidelines. Manuscripts were anonymized by removing identifying information and submitted to each model with a standardized prompt. Two investigators independently analyzed reviews for final verdicts, trial awareness, journal suitability assessments, and concerns across five domains (biological, methodological, statistical, trial groups, and reporting). Chi-square tests with Bonferroni correction and logistic regression were used for statistical analysis.
Significant differences were observed in reviewer verdicts among models (p < 0.001). Claude Sonnet 4.5 was most stringent (74% major revisions, 6% rejections), while Google Gemini 3.0 was most lenient (58% minor revisions, 4% acceptances). Trial awareness varied significantly (Claude 54%, Gemini 50%, ChatGPT 14%; p < 0.001). Methodological concerns differed among models (Claude 86%, ChatGPT 80%, Gemini 62%; p = 0.014). Logistic regression identified statistical concerns as the only significant predictor of critical verdicts (OR = 8.57; 95% CI 1.28-57.4; p = 0.027). Journal suitability was assessed by Claude in 90% of reviews but by Gemini in none.
LLMs demonstrate heterogeneous performance in peer-reviewing landmark oncology trials, with significant variation in stringency, trial recognition, and methodological scrutiny. These findings highlight the need for standardized frameworks before integrating AI into peer-review processes.

title: Benchmark Accuracy Does Not Transfer: Domain Adaptive Deep Learning for Diabetic Retinopathy Detection in a Bangladeshi Clinical Setting.
authors: Riad Hossain; Ittekhar Mahin Abir; Ayesha Banu; Mohammed Nazim Uddin
journal: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
abstract: Deep learning could make diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening more accessible where ophthalmologists are scarce, but high benchmark accuracy does not guarantee reliable clinical performance. We investigate this gap using 3662 images from APTOS 2019 for source training and a balanced evaluation corpus of 500 fundus images (250 DR, 250 No-DR) from a Bangladeshi clinic, graded by a single experienced ophthalmologist. Source-trained models achieved 94.26-96.80% accuracy under tenfold cross-validation on APTOS, yet achieved only 49.4-50.6% (mean 50.0%) when applied directly to the clinical images. The resulting 44.46-46.85 percentage-point losses across all six architectures provide consistent quantitative evidence of severe domain shift. A full-cohort feature comparison yielded a classical-feature Fréchet distance of 133.49 and an MMD   2  of 0.3967 (permutation p = 0.0005  ). To recover target-domain performance, we evaluate an adaptation pipeline that integrates retinal-specific preprocessing, progressive fine-tuning with discriminative learning rates, soft-voting inference, and test-time augmentation. Aggregated out-of-fold evaluation produced 81.0% accuracy (95% Wilson CI 77.3-84.2%), 70.0% sensitivity, 92.0% specificity, 89.7% precision, and a 78.7% F1 score. Fine-tuning increased mean individual-model accuracy by 27.1 percentage points, whereas preprocessing contributed a descriptive 2.0-point increase. These findings quantify a substantial benchmark-to-clinic gap and show that target-domain adaptation can improve performance, while the remaining false-negative rate and single-clinic design preclude claims of clinical readiness.

title: ConvFormer3D: A Hybrid 3D-CNN-Transformer Front-End for Cine cMRI View Classification Pipelines.
authors: Nafiseh Ghaffar Nia; Vinesh Appadurai; Suchithra V; Chinmay Rane; Daniel Pittman; James Carr; Adrienne Kline
journal: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
abstract: It is vital to reliably identify the views of standard cine cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cine cMRI), since each determines which cardiac anatomy will be observed and undergo quantitative analysis. If the view is incorrectly identified, whether by a human observer or by an automated system, errors can propagate into subsequent analyses that give rise to the volumetric assessment, strain analysis, evaluation of the valves, and thus diagnostics. Accurate classification remains a challenge due to clinical variation between scanner manufacturers, differences in acquisition protocols, and motion artifacts. This study presents ConvFormer3D, a hybrid spatiotemporal architecture that includes a Kinetics-400-pretrained 3D residual encoder (R3D-18), modified to handle single-channel cine input, combined with a lightweight temporal transformer and attention-based token pooling. The convolutional stages supply local anatomical and motion priors, while the temporal transformer captures time dependencies throughout the cardiac cycle at full temporal resolution. The network is trained using deep auxiliary supervision, label smoothing, an exponential moving average of the parameters, and mixed-precision optimization. The model's predicted probabilities are then calibrated by temperature scaling. To prevent data leakage, the different partitions are created at the level of the individual patient, and all reported metrics are recorded at patient-clustered bootstraps at the 95% confidence interval, together with formal paired significance testing between the various models. On a separate patient-level test partition, ConvFormer3D achieved an accuracy of 0.983 and an expected calibration error of 0.003 after temperature scaling.

title: A curated dataset for cryo-EM map post-processing.
authors: Andreea V Florea; Rubén Sánchez-García; José A Gómez-Pedrero; Águeda Sierra; José Alonso; Javier Vargas
abstract: Cryogenic-sample Electron Microscopy (cryo-EM) has become a fundamental technique in structural biology, yet the assessment of post-processing methods remains challenging due to the lack of standardized and reproducible resources. Here, we present a curated dataset-carefully divided into non-overlapping training, validation, and test subsets-that includes half-maps, average maps, fitted atomic models, and post-processed volumes generated with diverse approaches, including Deep Learning methods such as CryoTEN, EMReady, EMReady2, and DeepEMhancer. Precomputed quality metrics derived from Phenix tools, and Q-scores are also provided, enabling quantitative evaluation of map-model agreement as well as global and local structural quality across different post-processing methods. This standardized resource enables independent and reproducible comparison of cryo-EM post-processing methods by the community. In addition, we provide a unified workflow and the code used for metric computation, allowing reproducible and consistent evaluation and facilitating the assessment of new methods. Overall, this dataset and evaluation framework provide a standardized reference for comparative studies and support the development of new cryo-EM map enhancement strategies.

title: Machine learning methods to decipher the evolutionary dynamics of microbial pathogens.
authors: Manolo F Perez; Anna Zhukova; Renny Doig; Olivier Gascuel; Caroline Colijn
abstract: We are currently witnessing an unprecedented rise in the amount of diverse data on pathogens and epidemics. These data include genomic sequences with metadata such as geographic locations, risk groups, and sampling information. Machine learning (ML) has been applied to overcome the scalability bottlenecks inherent in these heterogeneous and high-dimensional datasets. This review highlights how ML tools are achieving concrete successes in predicting pathogen adaptation and drug resistance, performing source and host prediction, identifying high-risk lineages, and estimating phylodynamic and epidemiological parameters. We also show how ML is transitioning molecular epidemiology from a retrospective monitoring field to a proactive and predictive framework for major global microbial threats. Finally, we discuss the limitations of these approaches with respect to interpretability, uncertainty estimation, data volume requirements, and model misspecification.

title: RELATION OF HEART WEIGHT WITH AGE AND WEIGHT OF CADAVER
authors: Jolly Agarwal; Virendra Kumar
abstract: Introduction: Height, weight, and age of person has significant impact on the normal size of heart. These parameters need to be considered when cut-off values indicating the need for treatment or even surgery are established. The aim of present work is to study the relation of weight of the heart with age and weight of cadaver. Material and Methods: The study was performed in the Department of Anatomy, Shri Ram Murti Smarak Institute of Medical Sciences, Bareilly on 30 hearts from embalmed cadavers. The hearts were procured from the cadavers available in our department. The heart was thoroughly cleaned and measurements were taken. Results: The mean heart weight was 223.37 ± 57.78 g. Significant relationship between age of the cadaver and weight of the heart (p=0.0004), weight of cadaver and weight of heart (p=0.0001) was observed. Conclusion: The above study provides valuable data of the heart in our geographical location, which may be useful for cardiac surgeons and physicians.
