title: Forward Stroke Volume and Ejection Fraction Estimation in Mitral Regurgitation: A Computational Hemodynamic Approach
authors: Amirahmad Saeidi; Mobina Ghajar; Sara Tarkiani; Amin Ramezani
abstract: Abstract Mitral regurgitation (MR) is a common valvular heart disease in which con- ventional measures such as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) can be misleading, as they do not distinguish between effective forward flow and regurgitant volume. This limitation may result in underestimation of the true hemodynamic burden of the disease. In this study, we develop a computational framework based on a closed-loop lumped-parameter cardiovascular model to evaluate forward cardiac function in MR. The model incorporates a regurgitant pathway across the mitral valve together with flow calculations at the left ventric- ular outflow tract (LVOT), allowing estimation of forward stroke volume (FSV) and forward ejection fraction (FEF).The model was first assessed against published physiological reference values and then used to simulate different levels of mitral leakage. As simulated regurgitant fraction increased from 0% to 58.30%, FSV decreased from 65.35 to 51.37 mL and FEF from 60.22% to 35.21%, while LVEF increased from 60.17% to 84.40%. These results illustrate how increased LVEF can coexist with reduced forward output in modeled MR. Overall, the proposed approach provides a physiologically interpretable and computationally efficient tool for analyzing MR hemodynamics. The framework provides a research tool for investigating MR hemodynamics and compar- ing conventional and forward-flow-based measures. Further validation using patient-specific clinical data is required before it can be considered for clinical application.

title: Double Jeopardy: Acute Mitral Flail and Culture-Negative Endocarditis in Bicuspid Aortic Valve Stenosis - A Case Report
authors: Maia-Ioana Boureanu; Ileana Grigore; Amalia-Stefana Artenie; Ruxandra Cojocaru; Katherine Mohr
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital cardiac malformation, frequently causing accelerated valvular degeneration and premature aortic stenosis. Although often asymptomatic, incident dyspnea, angina and syncope indicate advanced disease requiring surgery. Sudden severe de novo mitral regurgitation (MR), resulting from structural leaflet abnormalities or functional ventricular impairment, introduces diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, rapidly complicating the clinical course. Case Presentation We analyse the case of a 52-year-old woman with known severe BAV stenosis, ascending aortic aneurysm and prior deferred elective surgery who presented to the emergency department with dyspnea and orthopnea. She recently completed three 7-day empirical antibiotic courses (amoxicillin-clavulanate, levofloxacin, clarithromycin) for a respiratory infection. Upon admission, inflammatory workup showed elevated C-reactive protein (13.3 mg/dL) with normal leukocytes (7,700/mm³) and negative blood cultures. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed severe MR caused by posterior mitral leaflet flail (rupture of three chordae at the P2–P3 segments) and a suspected mass on a ruptured chorda, pointing towards infective endocarditis (IE). Cardiac computed tomography showed mitro-aortic curtain thickening with peripheral calcifications and a central high-density area suggestive of an organized thrombus or chronic abscess. Fulfilling major Duke criteria (imaging and direct surgical inspection), intraoperative findings confirmed native aortic valve vegetations and a mitro-aortic curtain abscess, which was evacuated. Surgical intervention consisted of mechanical aortic valve replacement (Bicarbon Slimline), reduction ascending aortoplasty and mitral repair with two neochordae and an incomplete ring. Following a favorable recovery, the patient was discharged in stable condition on acenocoumarol anticoagulation, beta-blocker, diuretic and statin therapy. Conclusion This case illustrates the diagnostic challenges of culture-negative endocarditis masked by prior antibiotic therapy in patients with severe BAV stenosis and acute mitral flail. When blood cultures and imaging alone are inconclusive, intraoperative confirmation remains decisive. Timely multimodal evaluation and combined surgical reconstruction are essential to manage these complex multi-valvular cardiac infections.

title: When Everything Looks Like Amiodarone: Diagnostic Challenges in a Polymorbid Elderly Patient
authors: Maria  Teodora Mitocariu; Carina Maria Ciocan; Sofia Ioana Hanganu; Viviana Ioana Stativa
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction Amiodarone is an efficient antiarrhythmic drug, but can cause cumulative toxicity, including cutaneous, thyroid, pulmonary, hepatic, cardiac and neurological adverse effects. In older patients with multimorbidity and polypharmacy, these effects can mimic existing conditions and complicate diagnosis. Case Presentation A 74-year-old non-smoking woman with persistent atrial fibrillation, treated with electrical cardioversion and maintained on amiodarone for 7 years, presented with exertional dyspnea, palpitations, asthenia, fluctuating blood pressure and vertigo. Amiodarone dose was 200mg/day until September 2026, when it was reduced to 100mg/day, resulting in a cumulative dose of 518g. Patient history included heart failure, moderate mitral regurgitation, hypertension, type IIb hyperlipoproteinemia, osteoporosis, severe coxarthrosis and a recently diagnosed nodular goiter. Telemetry showed resting sinus bradycardia (48-54 beats/minute). She also had progressive sensory polyneuropathy and photodermatitis. The main diagnostic challenge was the intense blue-gray discoloration of the forearms and face, suggesting amiodarone-induced hyperpigmentation. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroid function were normal, and endocrinology review was recommended for the goiter. No skin biopsy was performed. Differential diagnosis ranged from argyria, chrysiasis, ochronosis to heavy-metal deposition, however without compatible exposure. Pigmentation from minocycline, phenothiazines or antimalarials was excluded. Methemoglobinemia was improbable with peripheral oxygen saturation of 98%, and cyanosis from heart failure was excluded by the localized distribution and absence of edema. Amiodarone-induced hyperpigmentation was the leading diagnosis, given the sun-exposed distribution, prolonged treatment and concurrent photodermatitis. Amiodarone was neither stopped nor replaced to preserve sinus rhythm. At discharge, bradycardia persisted and was considered iatrogenic along with neuropathy that improved slowly under gabapentin. Pigmentation persisted, slightly reduced in hospital, probably due to absence of sun exposure. Conclusion Blue-gray skin pigmentation in an older patient on long-term amiodarone requires a structured differential diagnosis, especially with review of medication and exposure history, to avoid premature case closure. Regular monitoring of thyroid function, heart rate, nerves and skin remains essential.

title: When Dyspnea Hides the Heart: A Case Report of Biatrial Appendage Thrombosis and Splenic Infarction Revealing Severe Dilated Cardiomyopathy
authors: Medeea-Andreea Florea; Amalia - Elena Potlog; Ilinca Foia; Sofia-Ioana Hanganu; Radu Amaziliței
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction Heart failure may present with predominantly respiratory manifestations, delaying recognition of underlying cardiac disease. We report severe dilated cardiomyopathy complicated by biatrial appendage thrombosis and systemic embolization. Case Presentation A 52-year-old man with chronic alcohol use and smoking had three hospital presentations within six weeks. The first two (Pulmonology, Infectious Diseases) featured recurrent fever, cough, chest pain, hypoxemia, and bilateral rales, treated as respiratory infections with transient improvement. Four days post-discharge, he presented with confusion, abdominal pain, exertional dyspnea, and dry cough. Evaluation revealed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, elevated NT-proBNP (7713 pg/mL) and D-dimer, hepatocellular injury, and cholestasis. Transthoracic echocardiography showed biatrial enlargement, LVEF 10%, severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, and a dilated inferior vena cava (32 mm). CT pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but revealed right (20 × 12 mm) and left (14 × 7 mm) atrial appendage thrombi, with pericardial and bilateral pleural effusions. Abdominal imaging revealed splenic infarction, suggestive of systemic embolization. With low-molecular-weight heparin and guideline-directed heart failure therapy, he improved, with resolving edema and restored sinus rhythm. Repeat echocardiography showed LVEF 15%. He was discharged stable on oral anticoagulation and heart failure therapy. Alcohol-related cardiomyopathy was suspected, although an ischemic etiology had not been excluded; coronary angiography was planned. Conclusion Biatrial appendage thrombosis is uncommon in atrial fibrillation. Symptom overlap, absent cardiac history, and a respiratory diagnostic framework likely delayed echocardiography. This case highlights diagnostic challenges of overlapping respiratory and cardiac manifestations in severe ventricular dysfunction, emphasizing early cardiac assessment in recurrent respiratory presentations. Recurrent fever and splenic infarction raised infective endocarditis as an important differential diagnosis. Although transthoracic echocardiography revealed no visible vegetations, the absence of blood cultures and transesophageal echocardiography precluded its definitive exclusion. Thrombus chronology and causality remain undetermined; long-term outcome is pending.

title: Mitral Valve Prolapse: A Not-So-Innocent Anomaly—Morphological Factors Linked to the Risk of Sudden Cardiac Death
authors: Viviana-Ioana Stativă; Sofia-Ioana Hanganu; Carina-Maria Ciocan; Maria-Teodora Mitocariu
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) affects 2–3% of the global population and is a leading cause of mitral regurgitation in industrialized countries. Although often considered benign, MVP may be associated with ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death (SCD), particularly in young, otherwise low-risk patients. Mitral annular disjunction (MAD) and myocardial fibrosis have emerged as potential markers of an arrhythmogenic phenotype, highlighting the importance of multimodality imaging. Case Presentation We retrospectively evaluated 30 patients with MVP, divided into two groups: 15 patients with MAD and complex ventricular arrhythmias and 15 matched controls with MVP, no MAD, and no ventricular arrhythmias. Mean age was 47 ± 16 years in the MAD group and 49 ± 21 years in the control group. All patients underwent comprehensive cardiological evaluation and multimodality imaging, including cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) and coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). In the MAD group, frequent premature ventricular complexes and sustained ventricular tachycardia were documented. Imaging revealed MAD measuring 7–13 mm, predominantly bileaflet prolapse with thickened, redundant leaflets, mitral regurgitation of variable severity and systolic inferolateral wall curling. CMR provided additional tissue characterization, identifying inferolateral late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), suggestive of myocardial fibrosis, in two representative cases. CCTA complemented the assessment through coronary anatomical evaluation. Conversely, the control group exhibited no documented ventricular arrhythmias and no significant MAD. Imaging predominantly showed preserved mitral annular continuity, minimal or absent disjunction, and less pronounced valvular abnormalities. Conclusion Therefore, MVP comprises a heterogeneous clinical and morphological spectrum, with MAD and myocardial fibrosis potentially identifying an arrhythmogenic phenotype. Multimodality imaging, particularly CMR with LGE, enables comprehensive tissue characterisation and refined arrhythmic risk stratification, supporting individualised patient management.

title: Prognostic Value of Right Ventricular–Pulmonary Artery Coupling in Mitral Valve Surgery and Impact of Concomitant Tricuspid Valve Repair
authors: Amila Kahrovic; Harald Herkner; Clemens Gangl; Robert Zilberszac; Iuliana Coti; Alfred A. Kocher; Martin Andreas; Daniel Zimpfer; Paul Werner
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: Background The prognostic impact of baseline right ventricular‐pulmonary artery coupling on clinical outcomes following mitral valve surgery with specific consideration of concomitant tricuspid valve repair remains uncertain. Methods A total of 214 patients who underwent mitral valve surgery and presented with moderate tricuspid regurgitation at the index procedure were included. Patients were classified after baseline right ventricular‐pulmonary artery coupling (impaired versus normal). The primary study end point was a composite outcome of all‐cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization. Secondary study end points included all‐cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization. Results Impaired right ventricular‐pulmonary artery coupling was observed in 112 patients (52%), while 102 patients (48%) had normal right ventricular‐pulmonary artery coupling. The rate of concomitant tricuspid valve repair was similar between study groups (50.0% versus 49.0%, P =0.886). Impaired right ventricular‐pulmonary artery coupling was associated with a higher hazard of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio 2.60, 95% CI 1.32–5.14, P =0.006), heart failure hospitalization (adjusted hazard ratio 3.29, 95% CI 1.27–8.54, P =0.014), and all‐cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 2.25, 95% CI 1.11–4.59, P =0.025) during follow‐up. Additionally, concomitant tricuspid valve repair in patients with moderate tricuspid regurgitation was associated with a lower hazard of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.26–0.80, P =0.007). Conclusions Impaired right ventricular‐pulmonary artery coupling is a predictor of adverse outcomes after mitral valve surgery. Concomitant tricuspid valve repair for moderate tricuspid regurgitation seems to be associated with improved outcomes.

title: Can Severe Coronary Artery Disease Fully Explain a Dilated Cardiomyopathy Phenotype? A Case Report
authors: Andreea Simiuc; Anna Maria Iuroaia
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Introduction Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular dilation and impaired systolic function, with a heterogeneous etiology including genetic, toxic, and inflammatory factors. Distinguishing ischemic from non-ischemic myocardial injury can be challenging, particularly when significant coronary artery disease coexists with potential toxic exposure. Case Presentation A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and compensated toxic cirrhosis presented with exertional dyspnea. He reported consuming approximately 1–2 glasses of wine at each meal over the preceding 15 years, with occasional beer or spirits consumption. Clinical assessment revealed tachycardia, lower-limb edema, diminished breath sounds and bilateral pleural effusions. NT-proBNP (4,874 pg/mL), GGT (504 U/L) and LDL cholesterol were elevated. ECG demonstrated tachycardia, supraventricular and ventricular ectopy and left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography revealed left ventricular dilation, severe global systolic dysfunction (LVEF 24%), diffuse hypokinesia and mild mitral regurgitation. Coronary angiography demonstrated multivessel disease: 50% left main, 75–80% left anterior descending, 90% left circumflex stenosis, and complete right coronary artery occlusion. Preoperative cardiac MRI confirmed left ventricular dilation, severe systolic dysfunction (LVEF 28%) and diffuse hypokinesia. Late gadolinium enhancement showed a mid-wall distribution in the basal interventricular septum, without myocardial edema or ischemic-pattern scarring, providing information relevant to myocardial viability. A 25-gene cardiomyopathy panel was negative, with no relevant family history. Treatment included sacubitril/valsartan, bisoprolol, empagliflozin, furosemide, statin therapy and alcohol abstinence. Holter monitoring detected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, prompting amiodarone. Surgical revascularization followed. Subsequently, congestion and symptoms resolved, and LVEF improved to 38%. Conclusion Despite severe multivessel coronary artery disease, the absence of ischemic-pattern myocardial scarring on cardiac MRI supported an alcohol-related cardiomyopathy. This case highlights the value of multimodality imaging in differentiating ischemic from non-ischemic myocardial injury. Ventricular functional recovery may reflect both sustained alcohol abstinence and recovery of hibernating myocardium following surgical revascularization, although their individual contributions cannot be distinguished.

title: Wnt MVD study
authors: Na Xu; Katherine Yutzey
abstract: Myxomatous valve disease (MVD) is the most common cause of mitral regurgitation, leading to impaired cardiac function and heart failure. MVD in a mouse model of Marfan syndrome (MFS) includes valve leaflet thickening and progressive valve degeneration. However, the underlying mechanisms by which the disease progresses remain undefined. In this study, we identified Wnt signaling is activated early in myxomatous valve disease progression. Inhibition of Wnt signaling by Dkk1 induction in periostin-expressing valve interstitial cells at 1 month-of-age prevents the initiation of MVD, but late Wnt inhibition starting at 2 months does not prevent MVD progression, suggesting that Wnt signaling contributes to MVD progression in a time-dependent manner and provides a promising therapeutic target for the early treatment of congenital MVD in MFS.

title: Anaesthetic consideration in Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement (TMVR) with LAMPOON procedure in mitral annular calcification: A case report
authors: Namrata Kothari; Maitri Shah
journal: Southeast Asian Journal of Case Report and Review
abstract: Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is an emerging treatment for patients with mitral valve disease which includes mitral annular calcification who are deemed high-risk for surgical intervention. However, left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction remains a significant complication. The Laceration of the Anterior Mitral Leaflet to Prevent Outflow Obstruction (LAMPOON) procedure has been developed to mitigate this risk by preemptively splitting the anterior mitral leaflet (AML) before TMVR. The anaesthetic anagement of TMVR remains underrepresented in the anaesthesia literature. Consideration of the procedural approaches, underlying patient pathophysiology, and potential complications allows for the construction of a plan for perioperative management. During lampoon procedure AML laceration causes sudden mitral regurgitation and may cause transient hypotension, wire manipulation increases the risk of arrhythmias and Ballon Inflation & Leaflet Traversal may cause possible transient LV dysfunction. Here, we present the case of a 75-year-old female with severe mitral annular calcification and moderate mitral stenosis with regurgitation, along with severe LV dysfunction. She underwent a successful transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) with a LAMPOON procedure.

title: Lautropia mirabilis-Induced Peritoneal Dialysis-Associated Peritonitis: A Case Report and Literature Review
authors: Shu‐Hui Liu; Yufen Yan; Changcan Hu; Xiuling Huang; Qing Liu; Yanfei Liu; Nan Jia; Chunhua Han
abstract: Background: Lautropia mirabilis is an uncommon Gram-negative facultative anaerobic bacterium primarily colonizing the oral cavity and upper respiratory tract. Peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis (PDAP) caused by this organism is exceedingly rare, with only three previously published cases. Case presentation: We report a 49-year-old woman receiving continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis who presented with cloudy dialysate and abdominal pain. Peritoneal effluent analysis revealed a leukocyte count of 16,522 cells/µL, with 85% polymorphonuclear leukocytes, accompanied by an elevated serum C-reactive protein level of 42.77 mg/L. L. mirabilis was isolated from the dialysate and identified using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Following intraperitoneal antimicrobial treatment with gentamicin and subsequently ceftazidime, the patient’s symptoms improved. No recurrence of peritonitis was documented during follow-up. A review of the three previously reported cases highlights similarities in clinical presentation but differences in microbiological identification and antimicrobial management. Conclusions: L. mirabilis should be recognized as a potential, albeit rare, cause of PDAP. This case highlights the value of appropriate culture conditions combined with molecular identification for detecting unusual pathogens and emphasizes the importance of integrating microbiological findings with clinical and laboratory responses when guiding treatment.

title: Primary Cardiac Sarcoma with Mitral Valve Invasion Complicated by Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura: A Surgical Dilemma
authors: Ashtyn P. Philipsheck; Tomer Z. Karas; Kevin Accola
abstract: Abstract Background Primary cardiac tumors are rare, comprising approximately 0.3–0.7% of cardiac tumors in autopsy series, and sarcomas are the most common primary cardiac malignancy. Most arise in the right atrium as angiosarcoma; left atrial undifferentiated high-grade sarcoma is distinctly uncommon and carries a poor prognosis with low rates of margin-negative resection. Concurrent immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) introduces a management conflict between hemodynamic urgency and prohibitive bleeding risk for which guidance is limited. Case presentation A 63-year-old retired firefighter who participated in World Trade Center (WTC) rescue and recovery operations presented with decompensated heart failure. Imaging demonstrated a mobile left atrial mass prolapsing through the mitral valve with severe functional mitral stenosis (mean gradient 15 mmHg). Concurrently diagnosed ITP, confirmed by bone marrow biopsy, produced refractory severe thrombocytopenia (nadir platelet count 24×10³/µL) that repeatedly delayed operative intervention while the lesion was considered possibly thrombotic. After intravenous immunoglobulin and platelet transfusion raised the count to 60×10³/µL, urgent left atriotomy with tumor debulking and bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement was performed. Pathology showed a 6.2-cm high-grade spindle cell malignancy with 28 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, MIB-1 index approximately 50%, absent lineage-specific markers, and a positive posterior left atrial margin, consistent with primary undifferentiated cardiac sarcoma. He recovered and received adjuvant gemcitabine–docetaxel, but developed cerebral, osseous, pulmonary, and diffuse intra-abdominal metastases by 5–6 months and died shortly thereafter. Conclusions This case demonstrates how a competing hematologic diagnosis can delay resection of an obstructing cardiac malignancy, and how a microscopically positive margin portends rapid progression in undifferentiated cardiac sarcoma. The temporal relationship between the new ITP and the subsequent tumor diagnosis raises the possibility of a paraneoplastic mechanism, which has been described in roughly a quarter of reported cases of ITP associated with solid tumors as an antecedent finding. The patient's WTC exposure history is documented for completeness; malignancies in this population characteristically present at long latency, but no association between WTC exposure and primary cardiac sarcoma has been established, and attribution is not possible from a single case.

title: Distinct designs, complementary strategies: Tendyne and SAPIEN M3 in transcatheter mitral valve replacement
authors: Zhaoyang Ye; Stephanie Sellers; David J. Meier; Tim Attmann; Xiling Zhang; Thomas Puehler; Nina Pommert; Jacob Voran; Won Kim; G. Warnecke; Derk Frank; Georg Lutter
abstract: Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) has emerged as a transcatheter treatment option for selected patients with mitral regurgitation (MR) who are unsuitable for surgery or transcatheter edge-to-edge repair. Among dedicated TMVR devices, the Tendyne and SAPIEN M3 systems are the two clinically approved tech platforms with CE Mark and FDA approval. We comprehensively dissect their distinct design features, procedural characteristics, clinical outcomes, and associated complication profiles. Furthermore, we evaluate their respective patient selection criteria and long-term prognostic implications to facilitate evidence-based clinical decision-making for patients with severe MR. Beyond current metallic prostheses, this review extends to the future horizons of TMVR, specifically highlighting the emerging paradigm of tissue-engineered valvular stents and biodegradable scaffolds as potential solutions to overcome current limitations in prosthetic durability and biocompatibility.

title: ASSESSMENT OF CARDIOVASCULAR AND IMMUNOLOGICAL PARAMETERS IN PREGNANT WOMEN WITH ARTERIAL HYPERTENSION
authors: Tamar Svanidze; M. Jgarkava; Tamar Saralidze
abstract: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are associated with maternal cardiovascular and immunological alterations. Investigation of macrophage–lymphocyte rosettes (MLR) formation in vitro provides additional information. Purpose: Our purpose was to assess cardiovascular changes and activity of immunocompetent cells in pregnant women with hypertensive disorders and to evaluate their dynamics during treatment. Methods: We observed 90 pregnant women aged 18-45y. Arterial hypertension was detected in 24, among them 4 women had preexisting hypertension, 8 had a gestational arterial hypertension, 12 – preeclampsia without other co-morbidities. All P underwent Ecg, echocardiography(TTE), lab tests and estimation of MLR formation in 72-hour blood leukocyte cultures. In healthy donors amount of MLR equals 37,4 ±2.2%, In the physiological pregnant women (ph P) MLR decreases to 22-30%. Elevated levels of MLR were observed in AH compared to healthy Pregnant. Previous studies showed that MLR in vitro increases significantly in P with stress and premature birth. We divided Pregnant women into 4 groups(gr): I- physiological pregnant P, II- P with preexisting hypertension, III- P with gestational arterial hypertension, IV- P with preeclampsia. Results: In I gr amount of MLR was in normal range for pregnant(18 – 29%), while it was moderately increased in II and III gr (30-40%) and significantly increased in IV gr (45-60%) indicating impending premature birth. Notable, that 3P with preexisting hypertension developed peripartum cardiomyopathy after 36 weeks of pregnancy. According to TTE mild mitral regurgitation was observed in 85% of physiological pregnancies, while 33% of pregnants with AH had mild MR and the rest 67% had moderate MR. Left atrial size was normal in physiological pregnancy, in pregnants with arterial hypertension it was normal or borderline increased, in 3 with preeclampsia it was increased. These 3P revealed PPCM with diastolic dysfunction -impaired relaxation, decreased ejection fraction and markedly increased NT-proBNP. In other P with AH or preeclampsia, EF was preserved. Diastolic dysfunction was observed only in 6 Patients with preeclampsia (50% of PE) including Pregnants with PPCM. After treatment and delivery, normalization of blood pressure, resolution of volume overload, and marked reduction of MLR up to normal range were observed. Conclusions: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are associated with increased MLR formation, reflecting activation of immunological processes. Reduction of MLR levels in parallel with clinical and hemodynamic stabilization, suggests its potential role as a marker for disease severity and effectiveness of treatment in addition to Echo data. Future studies in this direction is reasonable.

title: Transcatheter Mitral Cerclage Ventriculoplasty: 5-Year Outcomes
authors: Toby Rogers; Adam B. Greenbaum; Vasilis C. Babaliaros; Jason R. Foerst; Jaffar M. Khan; Christopher G. Bruce; Annette M. Stine; Xin Tian; Robert J. Lederman
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transcatheter mitral cerclage ventriculoplasty places a circumferential tensioning loop around the base of the left ventricle to reduce mitral annular dimensions and reshape ventricular geometry in patients with functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure. Early experience demonstrated reductions in mitral regurgitation and improvements in heart failure symptoms. METHODS: The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Division of Intramural Research Transcatheter Mitral Cerclage Ventriculoplasty Early Feasibility Study was an investigator-initiated, prospective, multicenter study. Between 1 and 5 years, vital status, serious adverse events, routine clinical documentation, and site-reported transthoracic echocardiography findings were collected. RESULTS: Nineteen procedures were attempted in 18 participants (63% heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, 37% heart failure with preserved ejection fraction). Median age was 73 years, and 63% were female. Kaplan-Meier estimated 5-year survival was 57%. One participant underwent left ventricular assist device implantation after 2 years, and 1 participant underwent mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair after 3 years; none underwent heart transplantation. The study was suspended after complete heart block developed in 6 participants, including 4 requiring new cardiac implantable electronic devices. Among participants with available follow-up echocardiography, site-reported imaging demonstrated mitral regurgitation reduction and improved left ventricular ejection fraction through 5 years. Symptomatic improvement was most apparent during the first year and attenuated thereafter. CONCLUSIONS: Cerclage ventriculoplasty was associated with mitral regurgitation reduction and improved ventricular function among participants with available long-term follow-up. Symptomatic benefit was greatest during the first year and diminished thereafter, suggesting that favorable remodeling may not fully offset progression of the underlying cardiomyopathy. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT03929913.

title: Introduction to transcatheter tricuspid valve intervention
authors: Lisa Serafini; Alessandra Ricci; Roberta Rosati; Marco Metra; Marianna Adamo
abstract: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) has historically been an undertreated valvular disease, but its management has evolved rapidly in recent years, particularly with the development of transcatheter tricuspid valve interventions (TTVI). Building on experience from the mitral field, dedicated devices targeting leaflet coaptation, annular remodeling, orthotopic valve replacement, and heterotopic caval implantation have been developed and are now clinically available. Randomized clinical trials, such as TRILUMINATE, Tri.Fr, and TRISCEND II, have demonstrated the feasibility and safety of these approaches, with consistent improvements in symptoms and quality of life. However, effects on hard clinical outcomes remain less clearly defined, partly due to modest sample sizes, heterogeneous populations, and reliance on composite and patient-reported endpoints. Large registries have provided valuable real-world evidence, underscoring—with respect to outcomes—the importance of procedural success and early referral before advanced right ventricular dysfunction occurs. Although optimized guideline-directed medical therapy remains fundamental, its impact on advanced TR is limited. Emerging data suggest a potential synergy between device therapy and medical treatment, as successful intervention may improve hemodynamics and facilitate guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) implementation and decongestion therapies may fecilitate TTVI Ongoing studies and refined trial designs will be crucial to define optimal patient selection, timing, and long-term outcomes in this expanding field.

title: Population-level emulation enables fast Bayesian calibration of cardiac digital twins
authors: Clara E Jones; Felix Plappert; Derek J. Bivona; Johane Bracamonte; Zarif Hossain; Isabella Aleman; Lyna Luu; Kenneth C. Bilchick; Pim J. A. Oomen
abstract: Purpose: Patient-specific cardiac digital twins have the potential to guide individualized therapy, but generating these in a routine clinical workflow remains challenging. This is especially true when the twins must carry quantified uncertainty: Bayesian calibration requires thousands of simulations per patient, and the emulators that reduce this cost are typically trained one patient at a time. We aimed to train a single emulator across a patient cohort, so that a new patient can be calibrated in minutes without new simulations. Methods: We trained a population-level Gaussian process emulator whose inputs included a 12-dimensional latent encoding of the clinical features of each patient, so that a single emulator represents the whole cohort. We compared spending simulation budgets on resampling the real cohort with augmenting the cohort with digital chimeras, synthetic patients interpolated between real patients. Seven parameters of a closed-loop heart and circulation model were calibrated by Markov chain Monte Carlo to ten clinical biomarkers in 26 patients with left bundle branch block, each using an emulator trained without that patient, and the calibrated posteriors were compared against the full simulator. Results: A single emulator, trained without the held-out patient, calibrated the digital twin of each patient in 59.7-63.0 s per patient, versus 15 h with the simulator. Resampling the real cohort was the more efficient training strategy, bringing every output to R2 greater than or equal to 0.9, which augmentation did not achieve for the same simulation budget. For held-out patients, both strategies performed comparably (median leave-one-out normalized root-mean-square error 11.0% vs. 10.7%; p = 0.745), and error rose with distance from the cohort centroid (Spearman rho = +0.406). The calibrated models showed no cohort-wide bias (median standardized residual -0.12 against the clinical targets), and 95% predictive intervals contained 78.5% of targets, with the largest misfit in systolic blood pressure. Conclusion: Removing the need for new simulations for every new patient is a meaningful step toward uncertainty-aware cardiac digital twins that fit within a routine clinical workflow. Because the simulator, surrogate and sampler are interchangeable, the approach used here can be applied to other (cardiac) models and cohorts.
